A Physicist’s Proof of the Lagrange-Good Multivariable Inversion Formula

Abdelmalek Abdesselam Affiliation: Département de Mathématiques Affiliation: Université Paris XIII, Villetaneuse Affiliation: Avenue J.B. Clément, F93430 Villetaneuse, France
Abstract\par

We provide yet another proof of the classical Lagrange-Good multivariable inversion formula using the techniques of quantum field theory.

Key words : Lagrange-Good inversion, Reversion, Quantum field theory.

I Introduction

The Lagrange inversion formula [Lagrange] is one of the most useful tools in enumerative combinatorics (see [GouldenJ, Stanley]). Various efforts have been devoted to finding purely combinatorial proofs and generalizations of this formula. One of the many such generalizations is the extension from the one variable to the multivariable case. Early contributions in this direction can be found in [Laplace, Jacobi, Darboux, Stieltjes, Poincare], but the credit for the discovery of the general multivariable formula is usually attributed to the mathematical statistician I. J. Good [Good]. We recommend [Gessel] for a clear and thorough presentation as well as for more complete references. Quoted from [Gessel] the Lagrange-Good formula says the following.

Theorem 1

Let the formal power series f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m} in the variables x1,…,xmx_{1},\ldots,x_{m} be defined by

fi=xi​gi​(f1,…,fm), 1≤i≤mf_{i}=x_{i}g_{i}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m})\ \ ,\ \ 1\leq i\leq m (1)

for some formal power series gi​(x1,…,xm)g_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}). Then the coefficient of

x1n1n1!​…​xmnmnm!inx1k1k1!​…​xmkmkm!​g1n1​(x1,…,xm)​…​gmnm​(x1,…,xm)\frac{x_{1}^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!}\ldots\frac{x_{m}^{n_{m}}}{n_{m}!}\ \ \ {\rm in}\ \ \ \frac{x_{1}^{k_{1}}}{k_{1}!}\ldots\frac{x_{m}^{k_{m}}}{k_{m}!}g_{1}^{n_{1}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})\ldots g_{m}^{n_{m}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})

is equal to the coefficient of

x1n1n1!​…​xmnmnm!inf1k1k1!​…​fmkmkm!×1d​e​t​(δi​j−xi​gi​j​(f1,…,fm))\frac{x_{1}^{n_{1}}}{n_{1}!}\ldots\frac{x_{m}^{n_{m}}}{n_{m}!}\ \ \ {\rm in}\ \ \ \frac{f_{1}^{k_{1}}}{k_{1}!}\ldots\frac{f_{m}^{k_{m}}}{k_{m}!}\times\frac{1}{det(\delta_{ij}-x_{i}g_{ij}(f_{1},\ldots,f_{m}))}

where

gi​j​(x1,…,xm)=def∂gi∂xj​(x1,…,xm).g_{ij}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{\partial g_{i}}{\partial x_{j}}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})\ \ . (2)

The odd-looking determinant in the denominator was probably one of the reasons this general formula was not discovered until [Good]. Remark however that a similar determinantal denominator appeared earlier in the classical MacMahon master theorem [MacMahon]. This is no coincidence since the latter is well known to be the linear special case of the Lagrange-Good formula.

We will use the quantum field theory model introduced in [Abdesselam1], which is related to an earlier formula of G. Gallavotti [Gallavotti] for the Lindstedt series in KAM theory, in order to express the compositional inverse of a power series in the multivariable setting. Our “proof” of the Lagrange-Good formula will follow from this representation of the formal inverse by straightforward and quite natural field theoretical computations which will, in particular, “explain” the determinantal denominator as a normalization factor for a probability measure. We warn the mathematical reader that reckless use will be made of wildly divergent integrals, if understood in the Lebesgue sense, and of quantum field theory terminology. However, when interpreted according to the formalism of our forthcoming article [Abdesselam2], our “proof” becomes a proof. Upon closer inspection, the reader who is familiar with earlier combinatorial proofs of the Lagrange-Good formula, like say in [Gessel] or [EhrenborgM], will undoubtedly have an impression of “déjà vu”. Indeed, the only connected Feynman graphs of our quantum field theory model are either a single tree or a collection of trees branching off a central loop. In fact, we provided the following “proof”, not so much for its originality, but for its entertainment value, as another instance of the magic of quantum field theory (see [Cartier]).

Aknowledgments : The content of this article is an outgrowth of techniques developed in collaboration with V. Rivasseau and presented in [Abdesselam1]. We thank J. Feldman for his invitation to the Mathematics Department of the University of British Columbia where part of this work was done. The pictures in this article have been drawn using a software package that was kindly provided by J. Feldman.

II The “proof”

First, we avoid the use of multiindices and write

gi​(x1,…,xm)=∑d≥01d!​∑α1,…,αd=1mwi,α1​…​αd[d]​xα1​…​xαdg_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m})=\sum_{d\geq 0}\frac{1}{d!}\sum_{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}=1}^{m}w_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}x_{\alpha_{1}}\ldots x_{\alpha_{d}} (3)

where the tensor element wi,α1​…​αd[d]w_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]} is completely symmetric in α1,…,αd\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}. Therefore the fi​(x1,…,xm)f_{i}(x_{1},\ldots,x_{m}) are the solutions of

fi=xi​∑d≥01d!​∑α1,…,αd=1mwi,α1​…​αd[d]​fα1​…​fαdf_{i}=x_{i}\sum_{d\geq 0}\frac{1}{d!}\sum_{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}=1}^{m}w_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}f_{\alpha_{1}}\ldots f_{\alpha_{d}} (4)

which can be rewritten as the direct reversion problem, with unknowns f1,…,fmf_{1},\ldots,f_{m},

yi=Γi​(f)y_{i}=\Gamma_{i}(f) (5)

with yi=defxi​wi[0]y_{i}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}x_{i}w_{i}^{[0]} and

Γi​(f)=deffi−∑d≥1∑α1,…,αd=1m1d!​xi​wi,α1​…​αd[d]​fα1​…​fαd\Gamma_{i}(f)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}f_{i}-\sum_{d\geq 1}\sum_{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}=1}^{m}\frac{1}{d!}x_{i}w_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}f_{\alpha_{1}}\ldots f_{\alpha_{d}} (6)

that is

Γi​(f)=∑d≥11d!​∑α1,…,αd=1mηi,α1​…​αd[d]​fα1​…​fαd\Gamma_{i}(f)=\sum_{d\geq 1}\frac{1}{d!}\sum_{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}=1}^{m}\eta_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}f_{\alpha_{1}}\ldots f_{\alpha_{d}} (7)

with

ηi,α[1]=defδi​α−xi​wi,α[1]fori,α∈{1,…,m}\eta_{i,\alpha}^{[1]}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\delta_{i\alpha}-x_{i}w_{i,\alpha}^{[1]}\ \ {\rm for}\ \ i,\alpha\in\{1,\ldots,m\} (8)

and

ηi,α1​…​αd[d]=def−xi​wi,α1​…​αd[d]\eta_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}-x_{i}w_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]} (9)

for d≥2d\geq 2, and i,α1,…,αd∈{1,…,m}i,\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}\in\{1,\ldots,m\}.

It was shown in [Abdesselam1] (see [Abdesselam2] for more detail) that the solution of such a reversion problem is given by the perturbation expansion of the following quantum field theory one-point function

fi=∫d​ϕ¯​𝑑ϕ​ϕi​e−ϕ¯​Γ​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y∫d​ϕ¯​𝑑ϕ​e−ϕ¯​Γ​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y.f_{i}=\frac{\int d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi\ \phi_{i}e^{-{\overline{\phi}}\Gamma(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y}}{\int d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi\ e^{-{\overline{\phi}}\Gamma(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y}}\ \ . (10)

Here ϕ¯1,…​ϕ¯m{\overline{\phi}}_{1},\ldots{\overline{\phi}}_{m},ϕ1,…,ϕm\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{m} are the components of a complex Bosonic field. The integration is over ℂm\mathbb{C}^{m} with the measure

d​ϕ¯​d​ϕ=def∏i=1m(d⁡(R​e​ϕi)​d​(I​m​ϕi)π),d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\prod_{i=1}^{m}\left(\frac{d(Re\ \phi_{i})d(Im\ \phi_{i})}{\pi}\right)\ , (11)

we used the notation ϕ¯​Γ​(ϕ)=def∑i=1mϕ¯i​Γi​(ϕ1,…,ϕm){\overline{\phi}}\Gamma(\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}{\overline{\phi}}_{i}\Gamma_{i}(\phi_{1},\ldots,\phi_{m}), and ϕ¯​y=def∑i=1mϕ¯i​yi{\overline{\phi}}y\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\sum_{i=1}^{m}{\overline{\phi}}_{i}y_{i}. If Ω⁡(ϕ¯,ϕ)\Omega({\overline{\phi}},\phi) is a function of the fields, we use the notation

<Ω(ϕ¯,ϕ)>U=def∫dϕ¯dϕΩ(ϕ¯,ϕ)e−ϕ¯​Γ​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y<\Omega({\overline{\phi}},\phi)>_{U}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\int d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi\ \Omega({\overline{\phi}},\phi)e^{-{\overline{\phi}}\Gamma(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y} (12)

for the corresponding unnormalized correlation function, and

<Ω(ϕ¯,ϕ)>N=def1Z<Ω(ϕ¯,ϕ)>U<\Omega({\overline{\phi}},\phi)>_{N}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{1}{Z}<\Omega({\overline{\phi}},\phi)>_{U} (13)

for the corresponding normalized correlation function, where the normalization factor is

Z=def∫d​ϕ¯​𝑑ϕ​e−ϕ¯​Γ​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y.Z\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\int d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi\ e^{-{\overline{\phi}}\Gamma(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y}\ \ . (14)

Finally we denote by <…>C<\ldots>_{C} the connected correlation functions, also known as cumulants or semi-invariants in mathematical statistics and probability theory.

Note that the “action” S⁡(ϕ¯,ϕ)=defϕ¯​Γ​(ϕ)−ϕ¯​yS({\overline{\phi}},\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}{\overline{\phi}}\Gamma(\phi)-{\overline{\phi}}y in the exponential can be separtated into quadratic and nonquadratic parts by writing

Γ⁡(ϕ)=C−1​ϕ−H⁡(ϕ)\Gamma(\phi)=C^{-1}\phi-H(\phi) (15)

with

[C−1]i​j=defηi,j[1]=δi​j−xi​wi,j[1][C^{-1}]_{ij}\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\eta_{i,j}^{[1]}=\delta_{ij}-x_{i}w_{i,j}^{[1]} (16)

and

H⁡(ϕ)=def∑d≥2∑α1,…,αd=1m(−1d!)​ηi,α1​…​αd[d]​ϕα1​…​ϕαd.H(\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\sum_{d\geq 2}\sum_{\alpha_{1},\ldots,\alpha_{d}=1}^{m}\left(-\frac{1}{d!}\right)\eta_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}\phi_{\alpha_{1}}\ldots\phi_{\alpha_{d}}\ . (17)

CC is the free propagator of our theory, ϕ¯​H​(ϕ){\overline{\phi}}H(\phi) is the interaction potential and ϕ¯​y{\overline{\phi}}y contains the sources which can be treated as particular vertices of the interaction. Therefore

e−S⁡(ϕ¯,ϕ)=e−ϕ¯​C−1​ϕ+ϕ¯​H​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​ye^{-S({\overline{\phi}},\phi)}=e^{-{\overline{\phi}}C^{-1}\phi+{\overline{\phi}}H(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y} (18)

and we let

d​μC​(ϕ¯,ϕ)=defd​ϕ¯​d​ϕd​e​t​C​e−ϕ¯​C−1​ϕd\mu_{C}({\overline{\phi}},\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}}{{=}}\frac{d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi}{det\ C}e^{-{\overline{\phi}}C^{-1}\phi} (19)

be the normalized complex Gaussian measure with covariance CC. As a result

Z\displaystyle Z =\displaystyle= ∫d​ϕ¯​𝑑ϕ​e−S⁡(ϕ¯,ϕ)\displaystyle\int d{\overline{\phi}}d\phi\ e^{-S({\overline{\phi}},\phi)} (20)
=\displaystyle= (d​e​t​C)​∫d​μC​(ϕ¯,ϕ)​eϕ¯​H​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y.\displaystyle(det\ C)\int d\mu_{C}({\overline{\phi}},\phi)\ e^{{\overline{\phi}}H(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y}\ . (21)

Now, by the standard rules of perturbative quantum field theory,

log⁡(∫d​μC​(ϕ¯,ϕ)​eϕ¯​H​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y)\log\left(\int d\mu_{C}({\overline{\phi}},\phi)\ e^{{\overline{\phi}}H(\phi)+{\overline{\phi}}y}\right)

is the sum over connected vacuum Feynman diagrams built using the propagators

            i        j    =Ci​j\hbox{}\hskip 0.0pt\raise-4.69772pt\hbox{\par \vbox to17.67pt{\vfill\hbox to50.59pt{\kern 0.0pt\hfil}\vskip-12.0pt\vskip 0.0pt\vskip-17.67pt\hbox to50.59pt{\hss}\vskip 13.43pt\hbox to50.59pt{\hskip 5.78pt\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$i$ \hskip-3.00003pt}\kern 0.0pt\vss}}\hss}\vskip-0.70999pt\hbox to50.59pt{\hskip 44.08pt\hbox to0.0pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$j$ \hskip-3.00003pt}\kern 0.0pt\vss}\hss}\hss}\vskip 4.95pt}}=C_{ij}

the HH-vertices

            i        α1        α2        αd    =−ηi,α1​…​αd[d]\hbox{}\hskip 0.0pt\raise-32.52127pt\hbox{\par \vbox to72.27pt{\vfill\hbox to72.27pt{\kern 0.0pt\hfil}\vskip-12.0pt\vskip 0.0pt\vskip-72.27pt\hbox to72.27pt{\hss}\vskip 37.94pt\hbox to72.27pt{\hskip 12.65pt\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$i$ \hskip-3.00003pt}\kern 0.0pt\vss}}\hss}\vskip-22.15001pt\hbox to72.27pt{\hskip 47.88pt\hbox to0.0pt{\hss\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\alpha_{1}$ \hskip-3.00003pt}\kern 0.0pt}\hss}\hss}\vskip 6.54001pt\hbox to72.27pt{\hskip 55.14pt\hbox to0.0pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\vss\hbox{$\alpha_{2}$ \hskip-3.00003pt}\kern 0.0pt\vss}\hss}\hss}\vskip 33.52pt\hbox to72.27pt{\hskip 47.52pt\hbox to0.0pt{\vbox to0.0pt{\hbox{$\alpha_{d}$ \hskip-3.00003pt}\kern 0.0pt\vss}\hss}\hss}\vskip 16.42pt}}=-\eta_{i,\alpha_{1}\ldots\alpha_{d}}^{[d]}

with d≥2d\geq 2, and the yy-vertices

These diagrams are made of a single oriented loop of HH-vertices linked by free propagators CC, on which tree diagrams terminating with yy-vertices are hooked. Since the sum over such tree diagrams builds the one-point function <ϕi>N=fi=Γ−1(y)<\phi_{i}>_{N}=f_{i}=\Gamma^{-1}(y), it is easy to see that

log⁡(∫d​μC​(ϕ¯,ϕ)​eϕ¯​H​(ϕ)+ϕ¯​y)=∑k≥11k​t​r​[C​∂H⁡(Γ−1​(y))]k\log\left(\par\int d\mu_{C}({\overline{\phi\par}},\phi)\ e^{{\overline{\phi\par}}H(\phi)+{\overline{\phi\par}}y}\right)\par=\sum_{k\geq 1}\frac{1\par}{k\par}tr{\left[\par C\partial H(\Gamma^{-1}(y))\right]\par}^{k}

where ∂H⁡(z)\partial H(z) is the matrix with entries ∂Hi∂zj​(z)\frac{\partial H_{i}\par}{\partial z_{j}\par}(z). Therefore

Z=(d​e​t​C)​e−t​r​log⁡(I−C​∂H⁡(Γ−1​(y)))Z=(det\ C)e^{-tr\log(I-C\partial H(\Gamma^{-1}(y)))}

or

Z−1\displaystyle Z^{-1} =\displaystyle= d​e​t​(C−1​(I−C​∂H⁡(Γ−1​(y))))\displaystyle det\left(\par C^{-1}(I-C\partial H(\Gamma^{-1}(y)))\right)\par
=\displaystyle= d​e​t​(C−1−∂H⁡(Γ−1​(y)))\displaystyle det\left(\par C^{-1}-\partial H(\Gamma^{-1}(y))\right)\par

∂Γ⁡(ϕ)=C−1−∂H⁡(ϕ)\partial\Gamma(\phi)=C^{-1}-\partial H(\phi)

so

Z−1=d​e​t​(∂Γ⁡(Γ−1​(y)))=d​e​t​(∂Γ⁡(f)).Z^{-1}=det\left(\par\partial\Gamma(\Gamma^{-1}(y))\right)\par=det(\partial\Gamma(f))\ .

Now we also have by ()

Γi​(f)=fi−(xi​gi​(f)−xi​wi[0])\Gamma_{i}(f)=f_{i}-(x_{i}g_{i}(f)-x_{i}w_{i}^{[0]})

Z=1d​e​t​(δi​j−xi​gi​j​(f))Z=\frac{1\par}{det(\delta_{ij}-x_{i}g_{ij}(f))\par}

which is our interpretation of the determinantal denominator in the Lagrange-Good formula as a normalization factor for a probability measure.

Γi​(f)−yi=fi−xi​gi​(f)\Gamma_{i}(f)-y_{i}=f_{i}-x_{i}g_{i}(f)

that is () becomes

with ϕ¯​x​g​(ϕ)=def∑i=1mϕ¯i​xi​gi​(ϕ){\overline{\phi\par}}xg(\phi)\stackrel{{\scriptstyle\rm def}\par}{{=}\par}\sum_{i=1}^{m}{\overline{\phi\par}}_{i}x_{i}g_{i}(\phi) and

ϕ1n1n1!​…​ϕmnmnm!inϕ1k1k1!​…​ϕmkmkm!​g1n1​(ϕ)​…​gmnm​(ϕ).\frac{\phi_{1}^{n_{1}}\par}{n_{1}!\par}\ldots\frac{\phi_{m}^{n_{m}}\par}{n_{m}!\par}\ \ \ {\rm in}\ \ \ \frac{\phi_{1}^{k_{1}}\par}{k_{1}!\par}\ldots\frac{\phi_{m}^{k_{m}}\par}{k_{m}!\par}g_{1}^{n_{1}}(\phi)\ldots g_{m}^{n_{m}}(\phi)\ .

which concludes our “proof”.
